newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore libel trial under human rights spotlight.
newsitem.headline: Singapore libel trial under human rights spotlight.

text.p: Singapore's leaders went to court again on Monday to accuse an opposition figure of defamation in a case being monitored by international human rights bodies.

"Amnesty International is concerned at reports that the Government of Singapore has used civil defamation suits against political opponents in a manner that violates their right to freely hold and peacefully express their convictions," the London-based organisation said in a statement.

The PAP leadership vehemently denies using the courts to silence the opposition. It was a question, Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said earlier this year, of challenging allegations of lying that would undermine his ability to govern.
In the second such case this year, Goh, his predecessor Lee Kuan Yew and nine other top members of the People's Action Party (PAP) are suing Workers' Party leader Joshua Jeyaretnam.

Both sides have brought in top London libel lawyers to argue their cases in a trial also being monitored by the Geneva-based International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) and which drew a huge crowd, with many people unable to get into the packed courtroom.

As in the first trial, the allegations stem from December's general election campaign when the PAP turned all its weapons on Workers' Party candidate Tang Liang Hong. The PAP romped to victory in 81 of parliament's 83 seats.
They accused Tang of being "an anti-Christian, Chinese chauvinist" who endangered racial harmony in predominantly ethnic Chinese Singapore, which has substantial minorities of Malays and Tamils.
Tang filed complaints to the police charging Goh and his colleagues with lying. They sued him, and Tang fled Singapore saying his life had been threatened.
He did not return to defend himself in the libel actions and the cases were won by the PAP leaders. The PAP leaders were awarded S$8.08 million (US$5.65 million) in damages.
They then sued Jeyaretnam, accusing him of endorsing Tang's charge of lying at the Workers' Party's last campaign rally.
"Mr Tang Liang Hong has just placed before me two reports he has made to police against, you know, Mr Goh Chok Tong and his people," Jeyaretnam told the rally.
That amounted to endorsement of Tang's charges, according to a prepared opening statement by Goh's legal team, led by London lawyer Tom Shields.

"The reaction of the crowd to the mention of the police report makes it clear that they were in no doubt as to what the defendant, himself an experienced lawyer and known to be such, was alleging," it said.
Jeyaretnam, who brought in libel expert George Carman to defend him, told reporters he would fight the case "all the way".
"I can't see those words meaning what they (Goh and his colleagues) say," he said.
Jeyaretnam has a long history of legal confrontations with the PAP, especially with Lee Kuan Yew, who was prime minister for more than 30 years.
Jeyaretnam has paid damages of more than S$780,000 (US$553,000) over the years to Lee.
In the most famous of Jeyaretnam's legal battles, he and a co-defendant were jailed for a month and fined S$5,000 in 1986 for making false statement over Workers' Party accounts.
The sentence disqualified Jeyaretnam from serving in parliament and from recontesting for five years.
He appealed to London's Privy Council, the highest court for many Commonwealth nations.
The council said Jeyaretnam and his co-defendant had been "publicly disgraced for offences of which they were not guilty", although the finding was only advisory.
Singapore later abolished appeals to the Privy Council.
